title: Bach in Stokowski’s orchestra
work: Toccata and Fugue in D minor, BWV 565 — opening
question: What happens to Bach’s opening flourish when an orchestra takes over from the organ?
intro: At Philadelphia’s Academy of Music on 6 April 1927, Stokowski recorded his orchestral version of Bach’s D-minor Toccata and Fugue. He gave the organist’s flourishes to a huge ensemble, including six horns, four trumpets and four trombones. Ninety years later, Norbert Schenk recorded the work on the church organ in Solms-Albshausen: one player commands the whole drama.

recordings.label: Leopold Stokowski, 1927
recordings.note: Stokowski conducts the Philadelphia Orchestra in his own transcription, enlarging the organ’s flourishes with a formidable brass section.

recordings.label: Norbert Schenk, 2017
recordings.note: Schenk plays the Protestant church organ in Solms-Albshausen; hands and feet supply the running notes and the bass beneath them.

passages.label: Opening gesture
passages.note: The opening flourish tumbles down in octaves, then stops. Silence punctuates the phrase as sharply as a chord.

passages.label: Gathering weight
passages.note: Notes accumulate into a held chord; the rushing line suddenly has something solid beneath it.

passages.label: Renewed surge
passages.note: Quick runs break away from the held chords. The toccata keeps switching between flying fingers and music brought to a standstill.
